chapter: On the road and into brass bands
title: Parade playing lessons from Teddy Riley
summary: Advice on pacing, alternating trumpets, and bouncing the sound off buildings.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Oh yeah, definitely. And I never forget, Thereto Riley gave me my first encouragement and lessons about playing a parade. And how to play a parade.
What did he tell you?
One of the first things is start off slowly so you don't blow yourself up.
Yeah.
We had three trumpets in the parade, in the band. So that meant two up and one down all the time.
What do you mean two up and one down?

That meant two people would play at once and one could take a rest. If the two people played three choruses, boom, you were resting three choruses. So you could come up with the next, you know, we're just vice versa, out of the tree trumpet players on how to do it. And there's another little secret is that when you're playing on the street, I shouldn't tell them young guys, but I'll tell them anyhow. What makes you sound nice and loud out there in the street is that you have to bounce your music off the buildings and the houses.
Well, that sort of comes naturally if you're in a, especially in the French Quarter.
Yeah, not if you don't know what to do.
So, but you consciously, what do you do? You direct it towards the...
Just turn to the side, left or right, and bounce it off. It comes back to the band and you loud as hell. Blow straight ahead and that's what's going on. It's just gone.
Yeah.
It's gone.
So if I see Milton Baptiste blow into the side like this... All the time. Blow into the side, yeah.
All the time.
Hmm.
All the time. Tell the rally. Give me that.
Hmm.
Yeah.
Hmm.
